To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the ultrastructure of STH (growth hormone) cells of castrated and of castrated, hepatectomised mice is different, and that the changes observed in hepatectomysed mice, with or without previous gonadectomy, are similar to each other.
STH cells of castrated mice show a higher rate of cell loss and an increased number of lysosome-like structures than STH cells of intact mice.
the STH cells of mice, after partial liver resection, show ultrastructural changes that may indicate an increased rate of secretion and a greater cell turnover.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ultrastructure of the STH cells of castrated mice after partial hepatecotomy.
the morphological differentiation between “castrated gonadotroph” and “post-hepatectomy” STH cells.
the ultrastructural features observed in STH cells after partial hepatectormy, with or without previous gonadal ablation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the present findings are compatible with the view that STH cells of castrated mice are capable of producing a hormone with the same chemical and biological properties as the hormone produced by STH cells in intact mice.
STH cells of castrated mice after hepatecotomy, although showing some ultrastructural changes, do not seem to be different from those of castrated or intact mice.
the ultrastructural alterations described in STH cells after hepatectomies are the result of a complex sequence of events that are not completely known.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the changes in ultrastructure observed in STH cells, in castrated mice with or without partial hepatectomies, could be interpreted as an increased rate of STH cell activity, with a subsequent increase in cell loss.

the STH cells are able to adapt to the new hormonal conditions, by changing their secretory pattern, but the changes observed in the present study suggest that this adaptation is not always successful.
the STH cells of posthepatectomized castrated mice show an increased rate of secretion of STH, a higher rate of cell loss, and a more active cell turnover than those of castrated mice.
The main takeaway from our work is that
hepatectomy, in addition to the previously reported changes, produces a number of ultrastructural alterations that are not observed in the pituitary after castration.
hepatectomy, in castrated mice, is a useful experimental model to study the ultrastructural changes that occur in STH cells after an increase in their secretory activity.
the STH cells in the pars distalis are not only able to produce and release growth hormone in response to the absence of gonadal steroids, but also to the removal of liver tissue.
